title: College on a Cattle Ranch
author: Aaron Renn
summary: This week's Aaron Renn digest covers three main topics. The lead essay profiles Deep Springs College, a tiny experimental school in the California desert where 26 students per year receive a free two-year liberal arts education on a working cattle ranch -- students legally own the institution, sit on the board of trustees, staff a volunteer fire department, butcher animals, and run admissions -- as a powerful counter-model to bureaucratized higher education that produces students with no stake in a common life. The second major piece summarizes a Financial Times analysis arguing that global fertility decline is now primarily driven not by couples having fewer children but by fewer young people forming couples at all, with smartphone adoption identified as the key inflection point in country after country. A third section analyzes Catholic vs. Protestant cultural capacity, drawing on Ryan Burge's data showing that even weekly-attending, politically conservative Catholics lag evangelical Protestants substantially on internalizing church teaching, with implications for which tradition can function as a 'human capital engine.' Renn concludes with a note on the Colbert cancellation as evidence that conservative cultural institutions chronically underestimate the talent and investment required to produce compelling media.
points: * Deep Springs College's model challenges the standard university: students legally own the institution, run admissions and curriculum committees, staff a volunteer fire department, and butcher cattle -- the key differentiator is that they have genuine stake in a common life, not the simulated community most universities advertise. * The NYT profile identifies the root of higher education's crisis as not merely political or demographic but existential: 'many of us live as collections of strangers, each pursuing our own ends, and our college education does almost nothing to develop the sense that what we do resonates with people beyond ourselves.' * The global fertility story has shifted: it is now less about couples having fewer children and more about the dramatic decline in young people forming couples at all -- a pattern that correlates tightly with smartphone adoption timing across countries ranging from France and Poland to Morocco, Nigeria, and Senegal. * Ryan Burge's data shows that even among weekly-attending, explicitly conservative Catholics, less than half believe pre-marital sex is always wrong -- a measure of how far official teaching has failed to penetrate lay belief, and evidence for Renn's broader claim that Protestantism has historically been a more transformational engine of human capital because it holds the laity to a higher standard. * Renn's observation about conservative cultural production is direct: the contempt for the bloated staffing of the Late Show misses the point -- producing compelling and impactful cultural products requires substantial talent and investment, and conservative institutions' chronic underinvestment is why their cultural impact remains limited.
quotes: 'We all, technically, legally own the place,' Will Xu told me last year. We were sitting at a picnic table on the campus of Deep Springs College, a tiny, experimental school in the California desert where he is a student. The college was founded in 1917 by a hydroelectric tycoon, L.L. Nunn. Today, Deep Springs educates about 26 students each year, offering them a free, two-year liberal arts education on a working cattle ranch.

These reflections are a start, but they ignore a core problem at the root of so many campus and social issues. It is not just that we lack civility and the capacity to respectfully disagree, but that many of us live as collections of strangers, each pursuing our own ends, and that our college education does almost nothing to develop the sense that what we do in our day-to-day lives resonates with people beyond ourselves.

In previous decades, the world's fertility rate went down because couples had fewer children. Now the main reason is that there are fewer couples. Had US rates of marriage and cohabitation remained constant over the past decade, the country's total fertility rate would be higher today than it was 10 years ago.

In country after country the birth rate plunged after the introduction of smartphones, no matter what the previous trend was. The younger the age group, the more pronounced the downturn -- a mirror image of smartphone usage patterns.

What I take away from all of this is that evangelical identity carries something that can't be fully explained by how often you show up or how conservative you vote. There's a theological and cultural foundation to evangelicalism that shapes how adherents think about the body, sexuality, and the family in ways that Catholic identity simply doesn't replicate -- even among the most devout and politically conservative Catholics.
